title: Short Stuff: Origin of Math Signs
summary: Short Stuff episode on the origins of the math symbols for plus, minus, multiplication, division, and equals. Josh and Chuck open with an algebra example from al-Khwarizmi's ninth-century book written out in words, then explain how symbols saved time. Robert Recorde is credited with the equals sign (from parallel lines in The Whetstone of Wit) and with introducing the minus sign to England. The plus sign is traced to the Latin "et," with Nicole Oresme's shorthand and competition from the Maltese cross. Luca Pacioli's P and M abbreviations are discussed as a possible source. The multiplication cross (St. Andrew's cross) is credited to William Oughtred, with an anonymous appendix in a 1618 logarithm book as earliest use. The division obelus is attributed to Johann Rahn (1659), and the solidus or fraction bar is noted as the ISO-preferred division symbol. The episode closes with a failed attempt to type the obelus with Alt plus numpad codes.

segments.title: Introduction and Latin word problem example
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic of origins of plus, minus, multiplication, division, and equal symbols. Chuck reads a word-problem style algebra example, which Josh says comes from al-Khwarizmi's ninth-century algebra book.

segments.title: Why notation mattered
segments.summary: Josh explains that the modern form of the algebra problem is x times ten minus x equals twenty one, and that symbols saved time in writing and teaching. Some problems were written as metered verse, which they call unnecessary, especially when writing with quill and ink.

segments.title: Equals sign and Robert Recorde
segments.summary: Chuck attributes the equals sign to Robert Recorde, a Welsh mathematician and royal court physician to Edward VI and Mary, who got tired of writing out 'equals' and proposed two parallel lines. Josh adds that Recorde wrote this in The Whetstone of Wit, which was influential in sixteenth-century math books, and says Recorde introduced the minus sign to England.

segments.title: Plus sign origins
segments.summary: The hosts explain that plus and minus come from Latin 'more' and 'less'. The plus sign is said to derive from Latin 'et' (and), and Nicole Oresme used it as shorthand. Its adoption took off in the sixteenth or seventeenth century, with competition from the Maltese cross, which was rejected for being slower to write.

segments.title: Pacioli's P and M and the minus sign
segments.summary: Chuck describes Luca Pacioli using a P and an M with a line over them for plus and minus. The M was apparently dropped, leaving the minus sign once a plus sign existed. Josh notes Recorde introduced the sign to England, and the hosts discuss the name of the line over the letter.

segments.title: Multiplication symbol and the Cross of St. Andrew
segments.summary: Chuck explains that the multiplication sign is called the Cross of St. Andrew, not a little x, because x already means an unknown in math. Josh jokes about the reaction at math conferences.

segments.title: William Oughtred and the first use of the cross
segments.summary: Josh credits William Oughtred, writing around the 1630s, with introducing the multiplication cross. Science ABC found an anonymous appendix in a 1618 translation of a logarithm book where the cross appears first, so the anonymous author is uncredited.

segments.title: Obelus and Johann Rahn
segments.summary: Chuck explains the division symbol with a dot above and below a line is called an obelus. Josh says it comes from a Greek word for sharpened stick and represents a small dagger, and credits Johann Rahn, a Swiss mathematician, with using it starting in 1659.

segments.title: Solidus and fraction bar
segments.summary: Chuck notes the slash-style division symbol is called a fraction bar or solidus. Josh says the ISO reportedly said only the solidus or fraction bar should indicate division and the obelus is out.

segments.title: Alt-code attempt for the obelus
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Science ABC's claim that the obelus can be typed by holding Alt and pressing 246 on the number pad. They try it on their keyboards and it does not work, so they suspect the tip is outdated and invite listeners to write in.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the short episode and invite listener feedback about the Alt-code trick.
